report:
**Conclusion: no—not on current evidence for people who already have osteoporosis.** Whole-body vibration (WBV) may improve balance, muscle function, or bone-mineral density (BMD) under some protocols, but it has **not been established as an effective fracture-prevention treatment** in osteoporosis sufferers.

The strongest fracture-focused review/meta-analysis in adults aged 50+ found that WBV *may* prevent fractures through fewer falls, but explicitly concluded that fracture effects require larger, adequately powered trials. That is not sufficient evidence to recommend it as a proven anti-fracture therapy.  
https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/7/12/e018342

Evidence supporting your view is indirect and qualified: a 2022 review reported reduced fracture risk in **healthy people without chronic illness**, and suggested WBV *may* be a safe supplementary treatment for osteoporosis. That population distinction matters: results in healthy participants do not demonstrate fracture prevention in people with diagnosed osteoporosis.  
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0965229922000139

There is more encouraging evidence for the surrogate outcome BMD: a systematic review of randomized trials in postmenopausal women found significant BMD effects, particularly with high-frequency, low-magnitude, high-cumulative-dose WBV. But higher BMD does not by itself prove fewer clinical fractures, and results depend substantially on device settings and dose.  
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00198-022-06556-y

A patient-focused osteoporosis organization likewise concludes that research is unclear on whether vibration therapy reduces broken-bone risk and notes that much research is in people *without* osteoporosis.  
https://theros.org.uk/information-and-support/treatments-and-medicines/complementary-therapies-for-bone-health/vibration-therapy/

WBV could be considered only as an adjunct to evidence-based osteoporosis treatment and appropriately prescribed exercise—not a replacement—after clinician advice, particularly if prior fractures, severe osteoporosis, balance problems, or spinal symptoms are present.
